Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Craft CMS passkey assertion replay: repeated POST to users/login-with-passkey
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Craft passkey replay: identical request-body size reposted to login-with-passkey · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Craft CMS passkey assertion replay: repeated POST to users/login-with-passkey AIExploitation Medium
Hunts byte-for-byte or rapid replay of a captured WebAuthn passkey login against Craft's native login-with-passkey action (GHSA-wg23-69c2-gjc8), where the stale challenge/counter lets one captured assertion body mint multiple sessions. A genuine passkey ceremony is a single successful POST; two or more successful POSTs to this endpoint from the same client within minutes indicates a replayed assertion. Rationale: Uses the article's exact Craft action path 'users/login-with-passkey' plus the stated one-per-ceremony property of WebAuthn to flag the replay: any repeat successful POST to that endpoint from a client is the captured bearer artifact being reposted. High-fidelity because the endpoint is single-purpose and a valid passkey login is not idempotent by design. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wg23-69c2-gjc8 • https://github.com/duo-labs/webauthn.io/issues/28
ATT&CKT1550 T1212 T1078
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User retries after a failed/cancelled passkey prompt, producing 2 POSTs in the same window
  • SPA/JS double-submit or browser auto-retry on flaky network
  • Multiple distinct employees behind the same NAT/corporate egress IP each logging in with a passkey
  • Synthetic monitoring / uptime probes hitting the login action
  • Load-balancer or WAF request duplication/retry inflating the count
Suppression filter
| where WindowSeconds <= 120   // tighten to near-simultaneous reposts; drop slow human retries
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the flagged cIP's full request sequence to login-with-passkey; compare csBytes (request size) and csUserAgent across the repeats — identical body size + identical UA within seconds strongly indicates a replayed assertion, whereas differing sizes/UAs suggest a legit retry. Identify which Craft account the resulting session belongs to. 2) Contain: force-revoke that user's active Craft sessions (admin > invalidate sessions / clear the users' auth), reset the affected account, and if confirmed, upgrade Craft to >= 5.10.5. 3) Hunt: review where the request body could have leaked (application/access logs, debug proxies, analytics/RUM scripts, browser extensions), and search web logs for any other account showing repeat successful login-with-passkey POSTs.
// Craft CMS passkey replay (GHSA-wg23-69c2-gjc8): >1 successful POST to users/login-with-passkey from one client in a short window
let Window = 10m;
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where csMethod == "POST"
| where csUriStem contains "login-with-passkey" or csUriQuery contains "login-with-passkey"
| where scStatus in (200, 302)          // Craft returns 200 (AJAX) / 302 on a completed passkey login
| summarize Attempts = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Statuses = make_set(scStatus), UserAgents = make_set(csUserAgent), Hosts = make_set(Computer) by cIP, csUriStem, bin(TimeGenerated, Window)
| where Attempts >= 2                    // 2 = a real ceremony is a single successful POST; repeats = replayed assertion body
| extend WindowSeconds = datetime_diff('second', LastSeen, FirstSeen)
| order by Attempts desc
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime, values(Web.status) as statuses, values(Web.http_user_agent) as user_agents from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method=POST Web.url="*login-with-passkey*" (Web.status=200 OR Web.status=302) by Web.src, Web.url, _time span=10m | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where count>=2 | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)` | sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime, values(Web.status) as statuses, values(Web.http_user_agent) as user_agents from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method=POST Web.url="*login-with-passkey*" (Web.status=200 OR Web.status=302) by Web.src, Web.url, _time span=10m | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where count>=2 | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)` | sort - count
Craft passkey replay: identical request-body size reposted to login-with-passkey AIActions on Objectives Medium
Complementary pivot for GHSA-wg23-69c2-gjc8 that keys on the request body itself: a byte-for-byte replayed WebAuthn assertion produces an identical request size (bytes received) to the same Craft passkey endpoint on 2+ requests, even if spaced apart or replayed from different source IPs. Distinct WebAuthn assertions carry fresh challenges/signatures, so a repeated exact byte-count to this single-purpose endpoint is anomalous. Rationale: Pivots on CsBytes (request-body size) against the article's login-with-passkey action: a replayed assertion is the same bytes, so an identical body length recurring on this single-purpose endpoint — especially across distinct source IPs — is the byte-for-byte 'reposting the same body' the advisory describes. Different pivot (body size + distinct-IP fan-out) than the time-burst rule. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wg23-69c2-gjc8
ATT&CKT1550 T1078
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Two different users' assertions that coincidentally serialize to the same byte length
  • Fixed-size error/JSON responses where the request body length is constant across failed attempts
  • A CDN/proxy normalizing or padding request bodies so sizes collide
  • Automated test accounts replaying a saved login request in staging
  • Very high-volume login endpoint where size collisions are statistically likely
Suppression filter
| where DistinctIPs >= 2   // focus on the same body length arriving from more than one client (replay from attacker infra)
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each colliding CsBytes group, confirm the requests carry the same or near-identical timing/UA and resolve which account(s) the sessions map to; a single account seeing the same body twice is high-confidence replay. 2) Contain: invalidate that account's Craft sessions and rotate credentials; patch Craft to >= 5.10.5 which persists the updated credential counter and rejects stale challenges. 3) Hunt: enumerate every request-body disclosure path (verbose app logs, debugging proxies, same-origin analytics/RUM, compromised extensions) that could have captured the assertion, and pivot on the involved source IPs across other auth endpoints.
// Craft CMS passkey replay (GHSA-wg23-69c2-gjc8): identical request body size reposted to users/login-with-passkey
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where CsMethod == "POST"
| where CsUriStem contains "login-with-passkey" or CsUriQuery contains "login-with-passkey"
| where ScStatus in (200, 302)
| where CsBytes > 0                       // bytes received = request-body size; a replayed body is identical in length
| summarize Requests = count(), DistinctIPs = dcount(CIp), SourceIPs = make_set(CIp, 20), UserAgents = make_set(UserAgent), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by CsUriStem, CsBytes
| where Requests >= 2                     // same exact body length POSTed >1x to the passkey endpoint = byte-for-byte replay candidate
| order by DistinctIPs desc, Requests desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Auth-passing inbound shipment/invoice email carrying a script or archive attachment · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Script-host JavaScript dropper spawning PowerShell from mail/download path · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Proxy config / AutoConfigURL modified by a scripting or loader process (banking-session interception) · [LLM] EtherHiding C2 resolution: non-browser process querying Binance Smart Chain RPC nodes · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Auth-passing inbound shipment/invoice email carrying a script or archive attachment AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound business-lure emails (shipment, invoice, scanned-document) that PASS SPF/DKIM because they were sent from a compromised legitimate corporate mailbox, and carry a script/container attachment (.js/.jse/.wsf/.hta or archive). This targets the Gen H1 2026 banking chain's initial access, where sender reputation and auth checks were satisfied by a hijacked account. Rationale: Uses the article's specific lure themes (shipment/invoice/scanned-document) plus the stated twist that SPF/DKIM PASS because delivery came from a compromised legitimate mailbox, combined with a script/container attachment type — the pivot generic phishing rules miss because they down-rank auth-passing senders. Cross-checked against: • https://www.gendigital.com/blog/insights/reports/threat-report-q2-2025
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1078
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate suppliers emailing genuine invoices/shipment notices as ZIP/PDF-in-archive
  • Internal automated scan-to-email MFPs sending 'scanned document' notifications with archive attachments
  • Logistics/booking platforms (DHL, Booking.com) sending real notifications that pass SPF/DKIM
  • Password-protected archive delivery from trusted partners for legitimate document exchange
Suppression filter
| where not (SenderMailFromDomain in~ ("dhl.com","booking.com","fedex.com") and FileType in~ ("zip","pdf"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: detonate the attachment in a sandbox; confirm whether the .js/.wsf executes a downloader or the archive nests a script. Check whether the sender domain is a known partner and whether that mailbox recently showed anomalous logins. 2) Contain: quarantine the message tenant-wide via NetworkMessageId, block the attachment SHA256, and if the sender is an internal/partner mailbox, force password reset + revoke sessions on that account. 3) Hunt: pivot to recipient endpoints for wscript/cscript executing the attachment name within minutes of delivery, and for the follow-on PowerShell and proxy-modification stages.
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound" and DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
| where Subject has_any ("invoice","shipment","scanned","scan","faktura","zasilka","z\u00e1silka","doda\u0301vka","dostawa","przesylka")
| where tostring(AuthenticationDetails) has "pass"   // SPF/DKIM passed despite malicious content (hijacked mailbox)
| join kind=inner (
    EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where FileType in~ ("js","jse","vbs","wsf","hta","zip","iso","img","7z","rar")
    | project NetworkMessageId, AttachName = FileName, FileType, AttachSHA256 = SHA256
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, AttachName, FileType, AttachSHA256, AuthenticationDetails
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.

// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
EmailEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound" and DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
| where Subject has_any ("invoice","shipment","scanned","scan","faktura","zasilka","z\u00e1silka","doda\u0301vka","dostawa","przesylka")
| where tostring(AuthenticationDetails) has "pass"   // SPF/DKIM passed despite malicious content (hijacked mailbox)
| join kind=inner (
    EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where FileType in~ ("js","jse","vbs","wsf","hta","zip","iso","img","7z","rar")
    | project NetworkMessageId, AttachName = FileName, FileType, AttachSHA256 = SHA256
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| project TimeGenerated, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, AttachName, FileType, AttachSHA256, AuthenticationDetails
| order by TimeGenerated desc
Script-host JavaScript dropper spawning PowerShell from mail/download path AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the Gen H1 2026 banking chain execution stage: a JavaScript/WSF dropper run by wscript.exe or cscript.exe out of a Temp/Downloads/Outlook-cache path that spawns PowerShell to fetch the next stage. Article-specific because the chain is attachment -> JavaScript dropper -> PowerShell stages, not an Office macro. Rationale: Anchors on the article's explicit chain 'JavaScript dropper -> PowerShell stages' via wscript/cscript parentage plus a script-file argument and a download/mail-cache launch path — distinct from the excluded Office-spawns-script and encoded-PowerShell rules. Cross-checked against: • https://www.gendigital.com/blog/insights/reports/threat-report-q2-2025
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1059.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate enterprise .vbs/.js logon or deployment scripts (SCCM, GPO) that call PowerShell
  • Software installers using a WSF/JS bootstrapper that invokes PowerShell
  • IT admin troubleshooting scripts run interactively from a Downloads folder
  • Vendor management agents wrapping PowerShell in a script-host launcher
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\ccmcache\", @"\SysWOW64\", @"\System32\") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("logon.vbs","deploy.js"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the parent script's full path and content; decode the child PowerShell command line for download/IEX activity and note the C2 URL. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the process tree, and block any resolved download domain/IP at the proxy. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for subsequent proxy-registry writes (Internet Settings\ProxyServer/AutoConfigURL) and new browser extension folders, and sweep other endpoints for the same script filename delivered by email.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (".js",".jse",".wsf",".vbs")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\Downloads\", @"\AppData\Local\", @"\INetCache\", "Content.Outlook")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ScriptHost = InitiatingProcessFileName, ScriptCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Child = FileName, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any (".js",".jse",".wsf",".vbs")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Script-Host JavaScript Dropper Spawning PowerShell (Gen H1 2026 Banking Chain)
id: 6f2a1c94-3b7d-4e21-9a8c-2f5b1d0e7a44
description: wscript.exe or cscript.exe executing a .js/.jse/.wsf/.vbs script and spawning PowerShell, matching the Gen H1 2026 banking-malware staging chain.
references:

level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\\wscript.exe OR *\\WScript.exe OR *\\cscript.exe OR *\\CScript.exe) @ParentCommandLine:(*.js* OR *.jse* OR *.wsf* OR *.vbs*) @Image:(*\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\pwsh.exe)

Proxy config / AutoConfigURL modified by a scripting or loader process (banking-session interception) AICommand & Control High
Detects the banking chain's session-interception step: WinINET proxy settings (ProxyServer, AutoConfigURL, ProxyEnable) written not by the Settings UI but by PowerShell, a script host, or a rundll32/regsvr32/mshta loader. This places the malware between the victim and their bank as the article describes ('modified proxy settings and installed a browser add-on'). Rationale: The article's distinctive banking-session-interception signature is proxy manipulation plus a browser add-on; writing WinINET proxy keys from a script/loader process (rather than the Settings UI or GPO) is high-fidelity because normal proxy changes come from explorer/settingsync/GPO, not powershell/mshta. Cross-checked against: • https://www.gendigital.com/blog/insights/reports/threat-report-q2-2025
ATT&CKT1112 T1090.001 T1176.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin PowerShell scripts that legitimately set corporate proxy/PAC (AutoConfigURL) during provisioning
  • Endpoint management tools (Intune/SCCM) applying proxy configuration via scripted actions
  • Developer tooling (Fiddler, corporate VPN clients) toggling ProxyEnable/ProxyServer
  • Login scripts pushing a PAC URL for web filtering
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Microsoft Intune Management Extension\", @"\ccmcache\") or RegistryValueData has_any ("pac.corp","proxy.corp"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the written RegistryValueData - a suspicious ProxyServer pointing at 127.0.0.1/high local port or an external AutoConfigURL is malicious; confirm the initiating process lineage back to the JS/PowerShell dropper. 2) Contain: isolate the host, revert the proxy keys, terminate the loader, and warn the user's bank if a banking session occurred while the proxy was active. 3) Hunt: enumerate installed browser extensions on the host, look for the parent script-host->PowerShell chain, and query other endpoints for the same proxy value or PAC URL.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\Internet Settings"
| where RegistryValueName in~ ("ProxyServer","AutoConfigURL","ProxyEnable","ProxyOverride")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\Local\", @"\Downloads\")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where RegistryKey has "Internet Settings"
| where RegistryValue in~ ("ProxyServer","AutoConfigURL","ProxyEnable","ProxyOverride")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

EtherHiding C2 resolution: non-browser process querying Binance Smart Chain RPC nodes AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the crypto-clipper's EtherHiding C2 step: a process that is not a browser resolving/connecting to Binance Smart Chain public RPC endpoints (bsc-dataseed*.binance.org, bsc.publicnode.com) to read C2 pointers from a smart contract. The on-chain pointer is takedown-resistant, so this behavioural network pivot outlives any single C2 domain IOC. Rationale: Keys on the article's stated EtherHiding-over-Binance-Smart-Chain C2 resolution and the corroborated public BSC RPC endpoints (bsc-dataseed*.binance.org, bsc.publicnode.com); a standalone non-browser binary issuing eth_call-style RPC to these nodes is the takedown-resistant behaviour that outlives domain IOCs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.elastic.co/docs/reference/security/prebuilt-rules/rules/macos/command_and_control_potential_etherhiding_c2 • https://www.endorlabs.com/learn/the-unkillable-c2-how-attackers-are-moving-command-and-control-to-the-blockchain • https://www.picussecurity.com/resource/blog/etherhiding-how-web3-infrastructure-enables-stealthy-malware-distribution
ATT&CKT1102.001 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate desktop crypto wallets (Exodus, Ledger Live, MetaMask companion) querying BSC RPC nodes
  • Web3 developer tooling (Hardhat, Truffle, Foundry, node.js dApps) hitting bsc-dataseed during builds/tests
  • Blockchain analytics or portfolio-tracker agents polling BSC public nodes
  • Browsers with wallet extensions proxying RPC via a helper process
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("exodus.exe","ledger live.exe","trust wallet.exe","node.exe","electron.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Program Files"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating binary and its path/signer - an unsigned EXE in a user temp folder querying bsc-dataseed while also monitoring the clipboard is malicious; a known wallet is benign. 2) Contain: isolate the host, dump and hash the binary, and capture the smart-contract address / RPC payload for on-chain pivoting (the contract data reveals current C2). 3) Hunt: correlate the same process with clipboard access and any outbound connection to the C2 domain the contract resolved; sweep the fleet for the binary hash and for other hosts querying the same BSC endpoints from non-wallet processes.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemoteUrl has "bsc-dataseed" or RemoteUrl has_any ("bsc.publicnode.com","bsc-dataseed.bnbchain.org","binance.llamarpc.com")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","iexplore.exe","vivaldi.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DnsQuery has "bsc-dataseed" or DnsQuery has_any ("bsc.publicnode.com","bsc-dataseed.bnbchain.org","binance.llamarpc.com")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

description: |

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

WordPress CVE-2026-64638 login-screen XSS payload in wp-login.php request AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound requests to wp-login.php whose username/query carries the parser-differential XSS signature described by pwn.ai: a tag opened with '<' immediately followed by whitespace (URL-encoded %3C%20 / %3C+ / %3C%09) so strip_tags() treats it as text but wp_kses_post() renders it as live DOM. This is the pre-auth initial-access step of the XSS2Shell chain. Rationale: Uses the article's exact parser-differential tell ('tag-like string containing whitespace after the opening <') expressed as its URL-encoded forms against the specific vulnerable endpoint wp-login.php; this is far tighter than a generic <script> XSS grep. Defender XDR ships no inbound web-access-log table so defender_kql is intentionally empty. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/security/advisories/GHSA-52p2-r8wf-jcrf • https://securityonline.info/wordpress-security-update-7-0-3/ • https://wordpress.org/news/2026/08/wordpress-7-0-3-release/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.007
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Automated vulnerability scanners (Nuclei, Burp, WPScan) firing XSS test payloads at wp-login.php
  • Legitimate redirect_to values that happen to contain encoded '< ' sequences
  • Bug-bounty researchers testing the site
  • Broken links where encoded HTML leaks into the login URL
  • Security-training/phishing-simulation platforms probing the login form
Suppression filter
| where HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent !has_any ("WPScan", "Nuclei", "Burp", "sqlmap", "nikto")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull full Url and HttpRequestHeaderReferer for the hit; decode the payload and confirm it opens a tag with trailing whitespace (< script). Check whether the source IP later hits authorize-application.php or wp-json on the same host. 2) Contain: confirm WordPress core is >= 7.0.3 (or the 4.7+ backport); if not, patch immediately and force-logout active admin sessions. Block the source IP at the WAF. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same SrcIp/UserAgent for /wp-json/ JSONP+_envelope calls, application-password creation, and new plugin ZIP uploads to confirm chain progression.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "/wp-login.php"
| where Url has_any ("%3C%20", "%3C+", "%3C%09", "%3c%20", "%3c+")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, HttpHostName, HttpMethod, Url, HttpRequestHeaderReferer, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, HttpStatusCode
| order by TimeGenerated desc

WordPress REST JSONP + _envelope=1 401-wrapping abuse (XSS2Shell execution) AIExploitation High
Hunts requests to /wp-json/ REST endpoints that combine a JSONP callback with _envelope=1. pwn.ai's chain uses REST JSONP to run attacker JS in the site origin and _envelope=1 to wrap an anonymous 401 denial inside an outer HTTP 200 so jQuery still executes the body as script. The combination of both parameters on the REST origin is highly specific to this technique. Rationale: Both _jsonp and _envelope=1 on a wp-json request is the article's named evasion primitive; legitimate WordPress clients almost never request JSONP wrapped in an envelope, so requiring both parameters together yields a low-FP alert. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/security/advisories/GHSA-52p2-r8wf-jcrf • https://securityonline.info/wordpress-security-update-7-0-3/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy JavaScript widgets legitimately using REST JSONP callbacks
  • Uptime/monitoring probes that append envelope parameters
  • Developer testing of REST responses in a browser
  • Third-party integrations reading wp-json with _jsonp for cross-origin embeds
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("127.0.0.1", "::1") and HttpHostName !startswith "staging"
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the callback name and target REST route in Url; check HttpStatusCode (expect outer 200 wrapping an inner 401) and whether the same session/IP loaded wp-login.php with an XSS payload just before. 2) Contain: verify core >= 7.0.3; block the source IP; force-reauth admins. 3) Hunt: from the same SrcIp/session, look for authorize-application.php approvals with external success_url and subsequent plugin uploads to confirm escalation.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "/wp-json/"
| where Url has "_jsonp=" and Url has "_envelope=1"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, HttpHostName, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

WordPress Application Password approval redirected to external success_url AIInstallation High
Hunts requests to /wp-admin/authorize-application.php where the success_url points to a host different from the site itself. In the XSS2Shell chain the origin XSS drives the native Application Password approval control so WordPress mints an API credential and redirects it to an attacker-selected HTTPS success_url, avoiding theft of the admin's primary password. Rationale: Targets the article's exact credential-access mechanism (authorize-application.php minting a credential redirected to an attacker success_url) and reduces noise by only flagging when the success_url host differs from the site host, which is the malicious variant. Sigma omitted because the host-comparison is a computed cross-field check. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/security/advisories/GHSA-52p2-r8wf-jcrf • https://patchstack.com/articles/wordpress-7-0-3-released-12-vulnerabilities-found-and-fixed/
ATT&CKT1098.001 T1212
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate third-party apps (mobile app, Jetpack, WooCommerce connectors) requesting Application Passwords with their own callback host
  • Developer registering an API integration with an external redirect
  • Password managers or SSO brokers on a different subdomain
  • Multisite setups where the callback host legitimately differs from the front-end host
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify which admin session approved the credential and the SuccessHost it was sent to; verify whether that app/host is a sanctioned integration. 2) Contain: in wp-admin > Users > Profile, revoke the newly created Application Password; force-reauth and rotate the admin's password; block SuccessHost egress. 3) Hunt: search for REST calls (Basic auth) from unfamiliar IPs/user-agents using the new credential, plugin-upload activity, and new administrator account creation immediately afterward.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "/authorize-application.php"
| where Url has "success_url="
| extend SuccessUrl = url_decode(extract(@"(?i)success_url=([^&]+)", 1, Url))
| extend SuccessHost = tostring(parse_url(SuccessUrl).Host)
| where isnotempty(SuccessHost) and SuccessHost != HttpHostName
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, HttpHostName, Url, SuccessUrl, SuccessHost, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, HttpStatusCode
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count from datamodel=Web where Web.uri_path="*authorize-application.php*" AND Web.uri_query="*success_url=http*" by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.uri_path, Web.uri_query, Web.http_user_agent, Web.status | drop_dm_object_name(Web) | rex field=uri_query "success_url=(?<success_url>https?[^&]+)" | eval success_host=replace(success_url,"https?(?:%3A%2F%2F|://)([^%/&]+).*","\1") | where success_host!=dest | sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where Web.uri_path="*authorize-application.php*" AND Web.uri_query="*success_url=http*" by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.uri_path, Web.uri_query, Web.http_user_agent, Web.status | drop_dm_object_name(Web) | rex field=uri_query "success_url=(?<success_url>https?[^&]+)" | eval success_host=replace(success_url,"https?(?:%3A%2F%2F|://)([^%/&]+).*","\1") | where success_host!=dest | sort - count
Malicious PHP file written under wp-content/plugins by web-server worker AIInstallation Medium
Hunts new .php files created under wp-content/plugins/ by the PHP/web-server worker process. In XSS2Shell the attacker uses the stolen Application Password to upload a ZIP that WordPress extracts into the plugins directory, planting an unactivated web shell that can be requested directly. Flags the file-drop persistence step on the host. Rationale: Anchors on the article's persistence step (ZIP extracted into wp-content/plugins, PHP requestable directly) and scopes to writes performed by the PHP/web worker, which is the malicious-upload path rather than an admin editing files on disk. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/security/advisories/GHSA-52p2-r8wf-jcrf • https://securityonline.info/wordpress-security-update-7-0-3/
ATT&CKT1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate plugin installation/update via wp-admin or WP-CLI writing PHP files as the web user
  • Scheduled auto-updates of plugins
  • Composer/deploy pipelines that run as the web user
  • Backup/migration plugins restoring plugin files
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("root") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "wp-cli"
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the new .php file's contents for eval/base64/system() and check whether it belongs to a known plugin slug; correlate the write time with an authorize-application.php approval and a plugin-upload REST call. 2) Contain: quarantine/remove the file, disable direct PHP execution from plugin dirs, and rotate any Application Passwords and DB credentials in wp-config.php. 3) Hunt: look for direct HTTP GETs to the new .php path, php-fpm spawning shell commands, and creation of rogue admin accounts.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FolderPath has "/wp-content/plugins/"
| where FileName endswith ".php"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("php-fpm","php","httpd","apache2","nginx")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFilePath has "/wp-content/plugins/"
| where TargetFileName endswith ".php"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("php-fpm","php","httpd","apache2","nginx")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

WordPress PHP worker spawning OS shell (web-shell command execution) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts php-fpm/apache/nginx worker processes spawning shells or network tools (sh, bash, curl, wget, python, perl, nc). This is the terminal impact stage of XSS2Shell where PHP is requested directly from the uploaded plugin and runs operating-system commands at the web worker's privilege level, exposing wp-config.php DB credentials and worker-readable secrets. Rationale: Targets the article's stated impact ('operating-system commands with that worker's privileges') via the high-signal LOLBin pair of a web/PHP worker parent spawning a shell/network tool child, which is almost never legitimate on a WordPress host. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/security/advisories/GHSA-52p2-r8wf-jcrf • https://securityonline.info/wordpress-security-update-7-0-3/ • https://wordpress.org/news/2026/08/wordpress-7-0-3-release/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Backup/migration plugins that shell out to mysqldump, tar, or rsync
  • Image-optimization plugins invoking imagemagick/exec via PHP
  • WP-Cron tasks launching curl/wget for scheduled fetches
  • SEO or CDN plugins calling external CLIs
  • Legitimate deploy hooks running as the web user
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has_any ("mysqldump", "wp-cron", "imagemagick", "convert ", "rsync")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture ProcessCommandLine of the child (look for reverse-shell, wp-config.php reads, credential dumping) and identify the parent PHP path/plugin; confirm the plugin is not a sanctioned one. 2) Contain: kill the process tree, isolate the host, rotate wp-config.php DB credentials and all Application Passwords, and remove the malicious plugin directory. 3) Hunt: review outbound connections from the worker to attacker infrastructure, new administrator accounts (wp_users), file changes to posts/pages, and the preceding authorize-application.php / plugin-upload activity.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("php-fpm","php","httpd","apache2","nginx")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","python","python3","perl","nc","ncat")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("php-fpm","php","httpd","apache2","nginx")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","python3","perl","nc","ncat")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Growing Up The Hard Way

The Hacker News
2026-08-07 5 use cases 4 techniques 3 kill-chain phases detected

Open Source had a great childhood. For two decades it got to be a kid. It ran around barefoot, gave everything away, trusted strangers, and never once thought about who was watching. It ran the kind of lemonade stand that took IOUs from anyone who wandered up — take what you need, pay me back whenever, no need to leave a name. It was idyllic. It was also, in retrospect, a little feral. Then,

Actions on Objectives
—
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

            - '\pwsh.exe'

Exposed hosts vulnerable to NatJack Windows NAT/Hyper-V origin-validation flaw (CVE-2026-56181) AIExploitation High
Surfaces Windows/Hyper-V hosts still exposed to the NatJack Windows NAT spoofing-from-adjacent-network flaw (CVE-2026-56181) so they can be prioritised for patching and untrusted-workload segmentation. Article-specific because it pins the exact CVE and the patched builds (24H2 26100.8875, 25H2 26200.8875, 26H1 28000.2525, Server 2025 26100.33158) rather than a generic NAT technique. Rationale: Pins the exact article CVE (CVE-2026-56181) and Microsoft's patched builds; TVM CveId is authoritative and avoids the ambiguous 26100-build revision math. No endpoint behavioural signal exists for the spoof itself because the NatJack forged response is NAT-rewritten to look like the legitimate peer. Cross-checked against: • https://www.networkworld.com/article/4206287/natjack-exploits-put-nat-security-assumptions-to-the-test-at-black-hat.html • https://www.synack.com/blog/malcolm-stagg-black-hat-2026/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/new-natjack-attacks-hijack-tcp-sessions.html
ATT&CKT1557 T1040 T1498
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • TVM inventory lag: host already updated to 26100.8875+/26200.8875+/28000.2525+/26100.33158+ but the vuln scan has not refreshed yet.
  • Hyper-V, WSL2, or Windows Sandbox not installed, so the vulnerable Windows NAT (winnat) driver is not loaded and the attack surface is absent.
  • Patch installed but pending reboot, so the running OSRevision still reports the pre-fix value.
  • Host sits on an isolated management VLAN with no untrusted workload sharing its NAT, so it is vulnerable-but-not-exploitable per the article's own precondition.
  • Gold/build-lab image flagged that never carries production traffic.
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm OSBuild/OSRevision is below the fixed level (24H2 26100.8875, 25H2 26200.8875, 26H1 28000.2525, Server 2025 26100.33158) and check whether Hyper-V/WSL2/Windows Sandbox NAT is actually enabled. 2) Contain: prioritise the KB rollout; where patching is delayed, move untrusted workloads off any NAT segment shared with the host and enable IP Source Guard on the access switch. 3) Hunt: enumerate other guests/hosts behind the same NAT, confirm internal traffic is encrypted (TLS), and review firewall/gateway logs for abnormal TCP RST/SYN bursts or DNS-response anomalies aimed at co-located hosts.

Exposed hosts vulnerable to NatJack Linux Netfilter conntrack SYN/RST teardown (CVE-2026-63913) AIExploitation High
Surfaces Linux hosts still on a kernel below the NatJack-fixed releases for the Netfilter conntrack direction-validation flaw (CVE-2026-63913), where a crafted SYN + invalid-sequence RST prematurely closes an active NAT conntrack entry. Article-specific because it targets the exact CVE and the fixed stable kernels (5.10.259, 5.15.210, 6.1.176, 6.6.143, 6.12.93, 6.18.35, 7.0.12, 7.1). Rationale: Pins the exact article CVE (CVE-2026-63913) and the kernel.org fixed stable releases; TVM CveId cleanly handles distro-backported version strings that a naive kernel-version compare would misjudge. The SYN-then-invalid-sequence-RST conntrack teardown is only observable in full packet capture / IDS, not in Defender/Sentinel/Falcon endpoint schemas, so exposure is the deployable pivot. Cross-checked against: • https://www.networkworld.com/article/4206287/natjack-exploits-put-nat-security-assumptions-to-the-test-at-black-hat.html • https://www.synack.com/blog/malcolm-stagg-black-hat-2026/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/new-natjack-attacks-hijack-tcp-sessions.html
ATT&CKT1557 T1040 T1498
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Running-vs-installed kernel mismatch: patched kernel is installed but the box has not rebooted, so the live kernel is still vulnerable (or the reverse false-positive after reboot).
  • Host does not use Netfilter NAT/conntrack (not a gateway, container host, or SNAT/DNAT router), so real exploitability is low.
  • Distro-backported kernels (RHEL/Ubuntu) whose version string looks older than the mainline fix but already contains the patch — scanner version-compare false positive.
  • Containers/network namespaces sharing one host kernel counted as multiple exposed assets.
  • Single-tenant NAT with no untrusted neighbour behind it, so the article's shared-NAT precondition is not met.
Response runbook
1) Triage: compare the running kernel (uname -r) against the fixed stable releases (5.10.259, 5.15.210, 6.1.176, 6.6.143, 6.12.93, 6.18.35, 7.0.12, 7.1) and confirm the host actually performs Netfilter NAT (iptables/nftables SNAT/DNAT or acts as a conntrack gateway). 2) Contain: schedule the kernel update + reboot; where delayed, separate untrusted workloads from the shared NAT and apply IP Source Guard. 3) Hunt: review firewall/conntrack and IDS logs for anomalous SYN followed by out-of-window RST against long-lived flows, and verify internal service traffic is TLS-encrypted so a hijacked conntrack entry yields no cleartext.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email

    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
