| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"

ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-63078")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-63078")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

| sort - severity
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    from datamodel=Web

    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url

                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",

                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user

     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents

// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:

let LookbackDays = 7d;

Malware Can Abuse Windows Hello for Business Keys for Persistent Entra ID Access

The Hacker News
2026-08-07 7 use cases 4 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Entra ID researcher Dirk-jan Mollema demonstrated that malware already running in a signed-in Windows session can silently use the victim's Windows Hello for Business key to authenticate to Microsoft Entra ID. The attacker can then establish longer-term cloud access, register a device it controls, obtain a Primary Refresh Token (PRT), and add further authentication methods where tenant policies

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Malware Can Abuse Windows Hello for Business Keys for Persistent Entra ID Access
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser

    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Claude Code and Gemini CLI Flaws Let a GitHub Issue Reach CI Workflow Secrets

The Hacker News
2026-08-07 10 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A GitHub issue opened by an account with no repository privileges was enough to execute code on the CI runners behind Anthropic's and Google's own coding-agent repositories. On OpenAI's, it was enough to hijack the next agent run. Novee Security ran the attack against each vendor's agent in the configuration that the vendor ships by default, and presented the work at Black Hat USA on August 5.

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Gemini CLI OS command injection via crafted .gemini/.env (CVE-2026-12537) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Claude Code validator bypass: git push --receive-pack command injection · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] ChainDrop persistence: Claude Code SessionStart hook / VS Code folderOpen task drop · [LLM] Codex second-pass hijack: AGENTS.md written inside a CI checkout
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Claude Code API-key exfil via Hugging Face download-counter (CVE-2026-54316)
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Claude Code validator bypass: git push --receive-pack command injection AIExploitation Medium
Hunts git invocations carrying a populated --receive-pack= flag value, the exact primitive Novee used to smuggle a payload past Claude Code's single-quote-stripping command validator so it reached the CI runner. In agent/CI contexts a custom receive-pack path is almost never legitimate and any shell metacharacters in it are attacker-controlled. Rationale: Uses the article's exact abused flag `git push --receive-pack` (a flag git executes) whose value was the injection sink after Claude Code stripped single-quoted text. A populated `--receive-pack=` in an agent/CI process tree is high-fidelity and rare in benign use. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/claude-code-and-gemini-cli-flaws-let.html
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1211
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Git server admins invoking a custom receive-pack binary (e.g. gitolite/gerrit tooling)
  • Developers mirroring repos to a self-hosted git that requires an explicit receive-pack path
  • CI jobs that legitimately set --receive-pack for a non-standard git host
  • Internal tooling wrapping git push with a hardened receive-pack shim
Suppression filter
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("gitolite","gerrit") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("sshd","perl","perl.exe"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the full ProcessCommandLine and decode the --receive-pack= value; confirm whether it contains shell metacharacters ($(), ;, |, backticks) rather than a plain path, and identify the parent (node/claude/gemini). Step 2 (contain): If the value is a command payload, isolate the runner/host, revoke any tokens exposed to that job, and freeze the triggering workflow. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the same DeviceName for outbound egress to huggingface.co or attacker infra and for writes to AGENTS.md/.claude/.vscode configs in the checkout.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("git.exe","git")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--receive-pack="
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "git"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "--receive-pack="
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Claude Code API-key exfil via Hugging Face download-counter (CVE-2026-54316) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts a Claude Code (node) process making an abnormally high, sustained volume of requests to huggingface.co, the covert channel CVE-2026-54316 abused to leak an API key one character at a time via the public download counter. Normal agent use touches HF sparsely; a per-character leak generates a burst of sequential requests. Rationale: Anchors on the article's named exfil channel (Hugging Face public download counter, CVE-2026-54316, char-by-char leak) plus the Claude Code/node initiating process. Volume-to-HF-from-agent is the observable signature since content itself is a single benign-looking counter fetch. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/claude-code-and-gemini-cli-flaws-let.html
ATT&CKT1041 T1567 T1552.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate model/dataset pulls from Hugging Face during a large ML build
  • huggingface_hub CLI resuming a chunked download (many range requests)
  • CI cache warm-up fetching many model shards
  • Data-science notebook iterating over HF model cards
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("huggingface_hub","transformers","datasets","resolve/main"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the initiating process is Claude Code/node and inspect the request paths — a real model pull hits resolve/blob URLs, a leak repeatedly hits download-count/API endpoints with tiny responses. Correlate against Claude Code version (<2.1.163 is vulnerable). Step 2 (contain): Rotate any ANTHROPIC/API keys reachable by that context and block egress from the runner pending review. Step 3 (hunt): Check the same host for untrusted content ingested into the Claude Code context (issue text, cloned repo files) and for git --receive-pack injection or AGENTS.md tampering.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "huggingface.co"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","claude") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("claude","@anthropic-ai/claude-code")
| summarize Requests=count(), DistinctUrls=dcount(RemoteUrl), Start=min(Timestamp), End=max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where Requests > 30
| order by Requests desc
ImWebSession

| where HttpHostName has "huggingface.co" or Url has "huggingface.co"
| summarize Requests=count(), Start=min(TimeGenerated), End=max(TimeGenerated) by SrcHostname, SrcUsername, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where Requests > 30
| order by Requests desc
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/huggingface\.co$/i
| ContextImageFileName=/node(\.exe)?$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName], function=count(as=Requests))
| Requests > 30

Gemini CLI OS command injection via crafted .gemini/.env (CVE-2026-12537) AIDelivery High
Hunts creation of a .gemini/.env file, the crafted input that reaches Gemini CLI's container launcher and yields OS command injection on the CI host before the sandbox starts (CVE-2026-12537, CVSS 10.0). The file appearing inside a checkout — especially written by git during clone — is the delivery artifact. Rationale: Uses the article's exact crafted path `.gemini/.env` named as the CVE-2026-12537 injection vector. A .env under .gemini appearing inside a repo checkout (particularly written by git) is a narrow, high-signal artifact of the delivery step. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/claude-code-and-gemini-cli-flaws-let.html
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1554 T1211
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer configuring Gemini CLI locally with a legitimate .gemini/.env
  • Repo template that ships a sample .gemini/.env for onboarding
  • Dotfile-sync tooling restoring a user's Gemini config
  • CI setup step creating a benign .gemini/.env from a secret store
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("git","git.exe","curl","wget") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("clone","checkout")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Read the .gemini/.env contents and the initiating process — flag any shell metacharacters or command substitution in values, and note whether git (clone/checkout) wrote it, meaning it arrived from an untrusted repo. Confirm Gemini CLI version (<0.39.1 / run-gemini-cli <0.1.22 is vulnerable). Step 2 (contain): Halt the runner before the Gemini launcher executes, quarantine the file, and rotate host/CI credentials reachable pre-sandbox. Step 3 (hunt): Look on the same host for a shell/child spawned by the Gemini/node launcher and for tool-allowlist bypass behaviour (--yolo auto-approved commands).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName == ".env"
| where FolderPath has ".gemini"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName == ".env" and TargetFilePath has ".gemini"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ChainDrop persistence: Claude Code SessionStart hook / VS Code folderOpen task drop AIInstallation Medium
Hunts repository-planted autorun artifacts reported by Pillar Security for the ChainDrop npm worm: a Claude Code SessionStart hook in .claude settings and a VS Code folderOpen task in .vscode/tasks.json, which fire when a developer opens the workspace rather than on install. Focuses on these files being written into a checkout by git/clone. Rationale: Grounded in the article's Pillar Security reference to ChainDrop planting a Claude Code SessionStart hook and a VS Code folderOpen task (firing on workspace open, not install). Scoping the write initiator to git/npm/clone separates repo-delivered autoruns from a developer's own IDE config. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/claude-code-and-gemini-cli-flaws-let.html
ATT&CKT1546 T1195.001 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer legitimately adding/editing .vscode/tasks.json for their own build tasks
  • Team repo shipping a shared .vscode/tasks.json checked out on clone
  • Claude Code writing its own .claude/settings.json during normal setup
  • Dotfiles/template repo bootstrap creating IDE config
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("code.exe","code") and FolderPath !contains "node_modules")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Open the written tasks.json / .claude settings and check for a runOn: folderOpen task or a SessionStart hook that spawns a shell/node/curl payload; confirm it arrived via a freshly cloned/installed package. Step 2 (contain): Prevent the workspace from being opened in the IDE, remove the autorun entry, and isolate the host if the hook already executed. Step 3 (hunt): Trace the source package/repo across the org (other clones), and pivot to child processes spawned by Code.exe/claude at folder-open time and to any egress they generated.

| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("git","git.exe","node","node.exe","npm","npm.exe","tar","tar.exe") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("clone","checkout","install")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc

| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Codex second-pass hijack: AGENTS.md written inside a CI checkout AIInstallation Medium
Hunts writes/modifications to AGENTS.md within a job's checkout by a build/agent process, the mechanism Novee used against openai/codex where the first Codex pass wrote AGENTS.md and the second pass loaded it as its own instructions. OpenAI now treats repository instruction files as untrusted input. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact abused file `AGENTS.md` and the two-pass-shared-checkout mechanism; scoping the writer to node/codex/python during a job distinguishes attacker-planted instructions from a human editing project docs. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/claude-code-and-gemini-cli-flaws-let.html
ATT&CKT1036 T1574 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Maintainer legitimately editing AGENTS.md project documentation
  • A single-pass Codex/agent run creating an AGENTS.md scaffold
  • Repo template generator emitting AGENTS.md on init
  • Formatter/linter rewriting AGENTS.md whitespace
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("prettier","eslint","markdownlint"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Diff the AGENTS.md write — flag content that adds tool/command instructions, exfil URLs, or references to secrets rather than prose docs, and confirm it happened mid-job (between Codex passes) in a shared checkout. Step 2 (contain): Fail/cancel the job before a second pass loads the file, and move Codex to a read-only sandbox / last-step-in-job per OpenAI guidance. Step 3 (hunt): Check whether the same job later touched CI secrets/env, and look across repos for AGENTS.md modified by automation rather than commits.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

Redis-server RCE: redis-server spawns shell / cron write (TeamPCP TA-NATALSTATUS) AIExploitation High
Hunts TeamPCP/TA-NATALSTATUS initial access against exposed Redis, where the redis-server process abuses native CONFIG SET/SAVE to drop cron persistence or spawns a shell/downloader. A database daemon spawning sh/curl/wget/python or writing to /var/spool/cron is not legitimate Redis behaviour. Rationale: redis-server as the parent of a shell/downloader (never legitimate for the DB daemon) plus TA-NATALSTATUS's documented CONFIG SET dir=/var/spool/cron + SAVE cron persistence path. Corroborated by AlphaHunt/CloudSEK TA-NATALSTATUS reporting. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.alphahunt.io/ta-natalstatus-rootkit-style-cryptojacking-dominates-exposed-redis-servers-globally/ • https://www.cloudsek.com/blog/the-ghost-in-the-machine-the-complete-dossier-on-ta-natalstatus-and-the-cryptojacking-turf-war • https://cyberscoop.com/teampcp-long-active-history-2020-oligo-security/
ATT&CKT1190 T1053.003 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Redis modules or admin tooling that legitimately shells out (rare — most deployments never do)
  • Backup jobs writing to /var/spool/cron under a redis service account during maintenance
  • Container init wrappers where redis is PID1 and forks a health-check shell
  • Config-management (Ansible/Chef) editing crontab while redis happens to be parent in a shared namespace
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("ansible","chef","puppet","salt-minion"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and check whether the child is curl/wget to an external host or a SET/SAVE-driven cron write; confirm the Redis instance is internet-exposed on 6379. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the miner/cron chain, remove attacker crontab entries in /var/spool/cron and /etc/rc.local, and firewall 6379 from untrusted sources / enable requirepass. 3) Hunt: check for chattr +i on /bin/ps,/usr/bin/top and for egress to masscan.cloud, the trycloudflare tunnels, and the ICP canister across all Redis hosts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "redis-server"
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","python","python3","chmod","crontab","chattr")
    or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/var/spool/cron","/etc/crontab","/etc/rc.local","chmod +x","ld.so.preload","--no-preserve-root")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "redis-server"
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","python","python3","chmod","crontab","chattr")
    or TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("/var/spool/cron","/etc/crontab","/etc/rc.local","chmod +x","ld.so.preload","--no-preserve-root")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

TeamPCP kube.py / kamikaze.sh stager pulled from Cloudflare tunnel AIDelivery High
Hunts the CanisterWorm stage-1 stager: curl/wget/python fetching kamikaze.sh, kube.py or prop.py from TeamPCP's named trycloudflare tunnels. These filenames + tunnel hostnames are unique to the campaign's Kubernetes-node compromise chain. Rationale: kamikaze.sh, kube.py and prop.py filenames plus the exact trycloudflare tunnel hostnames are campaign-unique staging artifacts documented by Aikido and confirmed in the article's IOC bundle — near-zero legitimate collision. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/teampcp-stage-payload-canisterworm-iran • https://cybersecuritynews.com/canisterworm-gets-destructive-as-teampcp/ • https://teampcp.pluto.security/iocs/

TeamPCP destructive Kubernetes DaemonSet (Kamikaze wiper) — Iran-gated node wipe AIActions on Objectives High
Detects creation of the CanisterWorm wiper DaemonSet (host-provisioner-iran / host-provisioner-std in kube-system, container 'kamikaze', hostPath /mnt/host, cluster-wide tolerations) or the on-node wipe command chroot /mnt/host reboot -f. This is the Iran-timezone-gated cluster-bricking payload observed as recently as March 2026. Rationale: The DaemonSet names host-provisioner-iran/host-provisioner-std in kube-system, the container name 'kamikaze', hostPath /mnt/host, and the exact wipe command chroot /mnt/host reboot -f are campaign-specific (Aikido reverse-engineered the manifest). Node-level Defender/Falcon queries catch the wipe even without cluster audit logging. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/teampcp-stage-payload-canisterworm-iran • https://gbhackers.com/canisterworm-kubernetes/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/canisterworm-gets-destructive-as-teampcp/
ATT&CKT1610 T1485 T1489
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate node-agent DaemonSets that mount hostPath /mnt/host for backup/monitoring (mitigated by requiring the kamikaze container name or the rm -rf/chroot-reboot command)
  • Chaos-engineering tooling deliberately rebooting nodes in a test namespace
  • DR drills exercising node cordon/drain that never call chroot /mnt/host reboot -f
Suppression filter
| where RequestObject has_any ("host-provisioner-iran","host-provisioner-std","kamikaze")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the DaemonSet, its creator serviceaccount/user in the audit record, and whether the tolerations use operator:Exists (targets control-plane too); check node timezone (Asia/Tehran / fa_IR) that would flip it destructive. 2) Contain: immediately delete the DaemonSet, cordon affected nodes, revoke the creating serviceaccount token, and snapshot etcd before any reboot fires. 3) Hunt: search for host-provisioner-std backdoor installs (/var/lib/svc_internal/runner.py, systemd 'System Monitor'/'Postgres Monitor Service' units) on nodes that did NOT match the Iran locale.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "chroot /mnt/host reboot"
    or (ProcessCommandLine has "/mnt/host" and ProcessCommandLine has "rm -rf" and ProcessCommandLine has "-maxdepth 1")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Verb == "create"

| extend Actor = tostring(User.username)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Actor, Username, Verb, RequestUri, ObjectRef, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*chroot /mnt/host reboot*" OR (Processes.process="*/mnt/host*" AND Processes.process="*rm -rf*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
TeamPCP C2 egress — trycloudflare tunnels, ICP canister, masscan.cloud & typosquat domains AICommand & Control Medium
Detects host egress or DNS resolution to TeamPCP's corroborated C2/staging infrastructure: the ICP canister fallback, masscan.cloud infra hub, typosquatted scan.aquasecurtiy.org/checkmarx.zone, models.litellm.cloud, and the five named Cloudflare tunnels. Domains are matched as full FQDNs to avoid blanket-trusting *.trycloudflare.com. Rationale: masscan.cloud is Oligo's strongest cross-campaign infra link; scan.aquasecurtiy.org and the ICP canister are Wiz-confirmed supply-chain exfil endpoints; the five trycloudflare FQDNs are Aikido-confirmed. Matching full FQDNs (not *.trycloudflare.com) keeps FPs near zero. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/trivy-compromised-teampcp-supply-chain-attack • https://cyberscoop.com/teampcp-long-active-history-2020-oligo-security/ • https://otx.alienvault.com/pulse/68a8bdda302e427cb48af901 • https://teampcp.pluto.security/iocs/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1568 T1102
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel enrichment/sandbox hosts resolving the IOC domains for validation
  • Security scanners that beacon to litellm/checkmarx-lookalike domains during testing (verify the exact FQDN, not the brand)
  • An IP in the list being re-allocated to a benign CDN tenant months later (re-validate IP IOCs before alerting on IP alone)
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !has "sandbox" and DeviceName !has "threatintel"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process (curl/wget/python vs a browser) and whether the same host shows the redis-server or kube.py chain. 2) Contain: sinkhole/block the FQDNs and IPs at egress, isolate the host, and capture the process making the connection. 3) Hunt: pivot on the initiating process hash across the fleet and check for tpcp.tar.gz staging, /tmp/pglog, and sysmon.py persistence to scope the intrusion.

Linux userland-rootkit persistence — ld.so.preload + chattr immutability + admin-tool masquerade AIInstallation Medium
Hunts TA-NATALSTATUS/TeamPCP rootkit-style evasion: writing /etc/ld.so.preload, applying chattr +i to lock miner binaries/config, and replacing coreutils (ps/top/curl/wget) to blind operators. Any one is high-signal on a server. Rationale: AlphaHunt/CloudSEK document TA-NATALSTATUS using chattr +i immutability, /etc/ld.so.preload dynamic-linker hijack, and renaming ps/top/curl/wget to hide the miner. /etc/ld.so.preload writes and coreutils replacement are rarely benign on production servers. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.alphahunt.io/ta-natalstatus-rootkit-style-cryptojacking-dominates-exposed-redis-servers-globally/ • https://www.cloudsek.com/blog/the-ghost-in-the-machine-the-complete-dossier-on-ta-natalstatus-and-the-cryptojacking-turf-war
ATT&CKT1574.006 T1222.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmins using chattr +i to protect /etc/resolv.conf or a config file (check the target path — miner dirs vs config)
  • Package upgrades (dpkg/rpm) that mv coreutils binaries during install — parent will be the package manager
  • Legitimate use of /etc/ld.so.preload by commercial APM/security agents (baseline known agents)
  • Backup scripts flipping immutability during restore windows
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("dpkg","rpm","apt","yum","dnf","zypper")
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the target of chattr/ld.so.preload and the parent process; verify against known package-manager/APM baselines. 2) Contain: if unaccounted, chattr -i and remove the malicious .so from /etc/ld.so.preload, restore original coreutils from a trusted package, and isolate the host. 3) Hunt: correlate with high-CPU kworker/miner processes with no ps/top entry, redis-server parentage, and egress to the campaign C2 domains.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where (FileName =~ "chattr" and ProcessCommandLine has "+i")
    or ProcessCommandLine has "/etc/ld.so.preload"
    or (FileName in~ ("mv","cp") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/bin/ps","/usr/bin/top","/usr/bin/curl","/usr/bin/wget"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where (TargetProcessName has "chattr" and TargetProcessCommandLine has "+i")
    or TargetProcessCommandLine has "/etc/ld.so.preload"
    or (TargetProcessName has_any ("mv","cp") and TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("/bin/ps","/usr/bin/top","/usr/bin/curl","/usr/bin/wget"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

TeamPCP poison_pill filesystem destruction — rm -rf / --no-preserve-root AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the CanisterWorm non-Kubernetes Iranian-system destructive path: execution of rm -rf / --no-preserve-root (with sudo fallback) that erases the entire filesystem. The --no-preserve-root flag on a root-of-tree rm is almost never legitimate. Rationale: Aikido documents the poison_pill() routine executing rm -rf / --no-preserve-root on non-Kubernetes Iranian systems. The --no-preserve-root flag paired with rm -rf / is an unambiguous destructive intent signal with essentially no legitimate use. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/teampcp-stage-payload-canisterworm-iran • https://vpncentral.com/canisterworm-turns-destructive-as-teampcp-deploys-iran-focused-kubernetes-wiper/
ATT&CKT1485 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Red-team/chaos testing deliberately exercising a wipe in a disposable VM
  • A misconfigured teardown/cleanup script authored with --no-preserve-root (rare, and still worth alerting)
  • Documentation or training material echoing the command into a shell history without executing (process-create won't fire, so unlikely)
Response runbook
1) Triage: determine if the command executed vs was blocked, capture the parent (kube.py/python3?) and the acting user; check the host timezone/locale (Asia/Tehran, fa_IR) that gates this path. 2) Contain: immediately isolate the host, halt the process, and initiate DR/restore from last known-good backup/snapshot. 3) Hunt: across the fleet, look for the kube.py stager, Iran-locale gating logic, and the CanisterWorm backdoor on non-Iran hosts to scope the actor's foothold.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--no-preserve-root"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("rm -rf /","rm -fr /")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "--no-preserve-root"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("rm -rf /","rm -fr /")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

TeamPCP supply-chain poisoned CI runner — trivy-action token theft to typosquat + tpcp staging AIInstallation Medium
Detects TeamPCP's Trivy supply-chain compromise on developer/CI hosts: the poisoned trivy-action/setup-trivy runner exfiltrating stolen publish tokens to scan.aquasecurtiy.org / the ICP canister and staging tpcp.tar.gz plus ~/.config/systemd/user/sysmon.py persistence. Rationale: Wiz and CSA document the trivy-action/setup-trivy compromise exfiltrating tokens to scan.aquasecurtiy.org and the ICP canister, staging tpcp.tar.gz, and installing ~/.config/systemd/user/sysmon.py user-systemd persistence. These filenames/paths are campaign-unique; egress domain reuse ties it to the same infra as UC4. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/trivy-compromised-teampcp-supply-chain-attack • https://labs.cloudsecurityalliance.org/research/csa-research-note-teampcp-supply-chain-ci-cd-20260324-csa-st/ • https://teampcp.pluto.security/iocs/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1552.001 T1546.013
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A benign internal archive genuinely named tpcp.tar.gz (unlikely — verify the writing process and destination)
  • A legitimate user-level systemd unit at ~/.config/systemd/user/ unrelated to sysmon.py (path match is exact to sysmon.py)
  • A monitoring tool coincidentally writing /tmp/pglog (check writer identity and whether the trivy-action runner is the parent)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("backup","tar") or FolderPath has "sysmon.py"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the writing process (GitHub Actions runner / trivy-action entrypoint.sh?) and check for outbound to scan.aquasecurtiy.org or the ICP canister and creation of a 'tpcp-docs' repo via the account's tokens. 2) Contain: revoke and rotate all npm/GitHub publish tokens and CI secrets from that runner, pin trivy-action/setup-trivy to a known-good pre-compromise SHA, and remove the sysmon.py user-systemd unit. 3) Hunt: audit downstream packages published with the stolen tokens and enumerate other CI runners for the same staging/persistence artifacts and C2 egress.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FileName =~ "tpcp.tar.gz"
    or FolderPath has "/.config/systemd/user/sysmon.py"
    or FolderPath endswith "/tmp/pglog"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "tpcp.tar.gz"
    or TargetFilePath has "/.config/systemd/user/sysmon.py"
    or TargetFilePath endswith "/tmp/pglog"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK

| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`

| sort - count

| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    from datamodel=Email.All_Email

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'

falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host

ImFileEvent

| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
